# Pesher Habakkuk — Reader's Guide
*HESED Reader's Guide | Dead Sea Scrolls Sectarian Texts*

---

## At a Glance

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Manuscript | 1QpHab (Cave 1, Qumran) |
| Language | Hebrew |
| Script | Jewish square script |
| Date of Composition | c. mid-1st century BCE |
| Date of Manuscript | c. 1st century BCE |
| Genre | Pesher — sectarian verse-by-verse biblical commentary |
| Canonical Text Interpreted | Habakkuk 1–2 (chapters 1–2 only; chapter 3 is absent) |
| Length | 13 columns; well preserved, one of the most legible DSS |
| Key Figures | Teacher of Righteousness, Wicked Priest, Man of the Lie (the Liar), Kittim (Romans) |
| Canonical Connection | Hab 2:4 ("the righteous shall live by faith/faithfulness") — quoted in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, Hebrews 10:38 |

---

## Sections Overview

**Columns 1–4 — The Chaldeans Become the Kittim**
The opening chapters of Habakkuk describe the terrifying rise of the Chaldeans (Babylonians) as God's instrument of judgment on a faithless people. The Pesher systematically identifies the Chaldeans as the Kittim — a term used elsewhere in the DSS for the Romans. The Roman legions are described in language borrowed directly from the Habakkuk text: they come swiftly, they take plunder, they fear no one, they are unstoppable. Column 6 specifies that the Kittim sacrifice to their military standards — an accurate description of Roman legionary practice, which treated the standards (signa) as sacred objects.

**Column 5 — The Liar and His Followers**
An extended section dealing with the "Man of the Lie" (also called "the Liar" or "the Spouter of Lies"), who led many astray from the correct interpretation of the Torah. He built a community on falsehood and opposed the Teacher of Righteousness. His followers are condemned.

**Columns 6–8 — Hab 2:2–4 and the Mystery of Faith**
This is the theological center of the pesher. The famous text of Habakkuk 2:4 — "but the righteous shall live by his faithfulness/faith" — is interpreted in column 8 to mean that the righteous live by their faithfulness to the Teacher of Righteousness. Salvation is tied to trust in and loyalty to the Teacher's interpretation of the Torah. This is the most theologically charged verse in the entire document.

**Column 7 — The Teacher as Revealer of Mysteries**
A crucial passage: God told Habakkuk to write things, but did not tell him the full meaning of what he wrote. The interpretation of the end times was not revealed to Habakkuk himself — it was revealed to the Teacher of Righteousness. The prophets wrote about the last days without knowing they were doing so; only the Teacher possesses the key to decode the prophetic word.

**Columns 9–13 — The Wicked Priest and His Crimes**
The most historically resonant section. The Wicked Priest is a high priest who began in righteousness but became corrupt — swallowed up by wealth and arrogance, defiling the sanctuary, and committing a specific outrage against the Teacher of Righteousness on the Day of Atonement. Column 11 describes the Wicked Priest pursuing the Teacher on Yom Kippur, apparently to the Teacher's place of retreat (possibly Qumran), disrupting his community's observance of the holiday.

---

## The World Behind the Text

**Habakkuk's original crisis.** The book of Habakkuk is dated to the late 7th century BCE, just before or during the rise of the Babylonian Empire. It is a dialogue between the prophet and God about theodicy: Why does God allow wickedness to go unpunished? Why does the law fail? Why does God use a more wicked nation (Babylon) to punish a less wicked one (Judah)? God's answer to the "righteous shall live by faith" passage (2:4) is essentially: the vision has an appointed time; be faithful in the waiting.

**The pesher genre.** Pesher (plural: pesharim; from the Hebrew root p-sh-r meaning "to interpret" or "to solve") is a distinctively Qumranic genre of biblical interpretation. It differs from other forms of ancient Jewish exegesis in one critical way: it applies the prophetic text directly and exclusively to the present moment and the community's own experience. Where other interpreters might ask what a prophetic text meant to its original audience, or what general moral truths it conveys, the pesher insists that the prophet was writing about now — about the Teacher of Righteousness, the Wicked Priest, the Kittim, the last days in which the community is living.

**The community's self-understanding.** The Qumran community — commonly identified with the Essenes mentioned by Josephus, Philo, and Pliny — understood itself as the faithful remnant of Israel, living in the end times, preserving the true interpretation of the Torah while the rest of Israel walked in darkness. The pesher method is the literary expression of this self-understanding: every prophecy that was ever uttered was ultimately about us, because we are the ones living at the end of history.

**The Wicked Priest controversy.** The identity of the Wicked Priest has been debated since the DSS were first studied. The most widely accepted candidates are Jonathan Maccabee (high priest c. 152–143 BCE) or his brother Simon (143–134 BCE) — Hasmonean leaders who began as heroes of Jewish resistance but who combined the offices of high priest and political ruler in ways many Jews found illegitimate. Other candidates include various Hasmonean and even early Herodian-period high priests. The text's language ("he was called by the name of truth when he first arose, but when he ruled over Israel his heart was lifted up and he abandoned God") fits the arc of a Maccabean leader who became corrupted by power.

---

## Why This Text Was Written

Pesher Habakkuk was written to confirm, for the Qumran community, that their situation had been foreseen and ordained by God.

The community had experienced what it understood as a profound crisis: persecution by a corrupt high priest, a schism in the Jewish leadership, the rise of foreign domination (Rome), and their own marginalized existence in the wilderness. The question pressing on any faithful community in such circumstances is: does God know about this? Does it make sense? Is there a way through?

The pesher answers yes — and proves it from the prophets. Every feature of the community's experience — the Teacher's persecution, the Liar's movement, the Roman military advance — was already encoded in the words of Habakkuk. This is not coincidence. It is divine providence, and it means the community is exactly where it should be, in the final drama that the prophets foretold.

The identification of the Kittim (Romans) is also a form of political theology. The Romans are not simply an arbitrary imperial power doing what empires do. They are instruments of divine judgment on a corrupt priesthood and a faithless people — just as the Babylonians were in Habakkuk's day. And the Romans' own judgment is also foretold: they will not escape.

---

## How to Read This Text

Read Habakkuk 1–2 first. Read it straight through. Notice the structure: the prophet complains, God answers, the prophet complains again, God answers again. The climax is 2:4 — "but the righteous shall live by his faithfulness." Then read what the Pesher does with each verse.

The pesher format is: the biblical lemma (a verse or partial verse quoted) followed by the interpretation, almost always introduced by the formula "its interpretation (pesher) concerns..." or "the interpretation of the word (pesher ha-davar) is..." The biblical text and the interpretation are formally separate, but the author treats them as two parts of one continuous divine communication.

Pay attention to the hermeneutical moves. When Habakkuk says "the Chaldeans" and the pesher says "these are the Kittim," the author is not making a mistake or claiming Habakkuk predicted Rome by name. He is claiming that "Chaldeans" was always a code word whose full meaning has only now become legible. The prophet did not know what he was writing about; the Teacher did.

Notice what the text does not say. The Wicked Priest, the Teacher, the Liar — none are ever identified by personal name. The text was written for a community that already knew who was meant. Modern readers must work backward from the descriptions to guess at identities.

---

## The Threads

**The Teacher as the key to Scripture.** Column 7 contains one of the most remarkable statements in all the DSS: God revealed to Habakkuk to write the things that would happen to the last generation, but the full meaning was not revealed to Habakkuk himself — it was revealed to the Teacher of Righteousness. The Teacher is not simply a wise interpreter; he is a divinely commissioned decoder. Without him, the prophets are sealed. This is an extraordinarily high claim for a human figure — and it anticipates, structurally, the claim that early Christians will make about Jesus as the one who opens the meaning of Scripture.

**"The righteous shall live by his faith" — three traditions, three meanings.** Habakkuk 2:4 is one of the most consequential single verses in all of biblical history. In its original context, it calls for patient faithfulness in the face of delayed judgment. At Qumran (1QpHab 8:1–3), it means living by faithfulness to the Teacher of Righteousness and his interpretation. In Paul (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11), it means justification by faith in Jesus Christ, received apart from Torah observance. In Hebrews 10:38, it grounds a call to persevere without shrinking back. The same three Hebrew words — emunatoh, "his faithfulness" — generated three profoundly different theological systems. Reading the Pesher alongside Paul is one of the most revealing exercises in the history of biblical interpretation.

**The Wicked Priest on the Day of Atonement.** The specific crime described in column 11 — that the Wicked Priest came to the Teacher's location on Yom Kippur to "confuse" or "swallow up" the Teacher and his community — is historically precise in a way that the rest of the document is not. The Qumran community observed a different calendar from the Jerusalem temple (a solar calendar versus the lunisolar calendar); this meant their Yom Kippur and Jerusalem's did not coincide. The Wicked Priest could travel on his own Yom Kippur (when he had no temple duties) to Qumran, where the Teacher's community was observing its Yom Kippur. This is one of the most specific and verifiable details in the entire DSS corpus.

**The Kittim as the Romans.** The term Kittim in the Hebrew Bible refers to Cyprus (and by extension, western maritime peoples). In Daniel 11:30, the Kittim arrive by ship and humiliate Antiochus IV — a reference that most scholars take as pointing to the Romans, who sent an ambassador to block Antiochus's invasion of Egypt in 168 BCE. The Pesher follows this identification and elaborates it with details that fit Roman military practice (sacrificing to standards, tribute from conquered peoples) with considerable accuracy.

**The Liar as a rival teacher.** The "Man of the Lie" (also "Spouter of Lies" or the "Liar") is a figure distinct from the Wicked Priest. Where the Wicked Priest is a corrupt institutional leader, the Liar is a competing religious teacher — someone who arose within or near the same movement as the Teacher, attracted followers, and led them into error. The community's self-definition runs against both figures: corrupt priestly power on one side, false teaching on the other. Some scholars have proposed the Liar may be a Pharisaic leader; others suggest he was an internal schismatic. The identity remains unknown.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

**The pesher is not allegory — it is apocalyptic code-breaking.** Modern readers sometimes assume that when the Pesher reinterprets the Chaldeans as Romans, it is doing something like allegorical reading — finding a general truth (God uses empires to judge) illustrated by a particular example. This is wrong. The Pesher insists that the prophet was specifically writing about the Romans, the Teacher, the Wicked Priest — the real, historically specific people of the last days. The biblical text is not an allegory whose moral we can extract; it is a coded message whose time has finally come.

**Habakkuk chapter 3 is not commented on.** The book of Habakkuk in modern Bibles has three chapters. The Pesher covers only chapters 1–2. Whether the Qumran community's version of Habakkuk did not include chapter 3, or whether the Pesher was intentionally limited to the two chapters most relevant to their theological concerns, is debated. The omission is notable.

**The Teacher's authority is greater than Moses' authority — functionally.** The Mosaic Torah is the foundation for the Qumran community, but the Torah requires correct interpretation, and only the Teacher has that. In practice, the Teacher's interpretation mediates access to the Torah's meaning. This is not stated explicitly in the Pesher, but it is the functional logic of the document. The same structure appears in early Christianity, where the apostolic interpretation of Scripture becomes the normative lens through which Scripture is read.

**The Wicked Priest may not always be the same person.** Some scholars argue that different references to the "Wicked Priest" in the Pesher may refer to different individuals — the Qumran community may have applied this title to a series of corrupt high priests over time. The document may layer episodes from different periods. This is contested, but the possibility should keep the reader from too quickly identifying all the Wicked Priest passages with a single historical figure.

**The scroll is almost certainly a sectarian production, not a general Jewish text.** Some DSS were in widespread Jewish circulation (biblical texts, 1 Enoch, Jubilees). The Pesher Habakkuk is almost certainly a Qumran community composition — its interpretive method, its reference to the Teacher, its specific historical allusions are all tied to this particular community's experience and self-understanding. It was not read outside the community; it was written for insiders who shared the community's worldview.

**Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 are in direct conversation with this hermeneutical moment.** When Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4 — "the righteous shall live by faith" — he is working with the same verse that the Pesher interprets. Paul's argument in Galatians and Romans turns precisely on this verse. Whether Paul knew the Qumran interpretation, whether his reading is a direct response to it, or whether both are independent responses to the same pressing verse is unknown. But reading Paul's interpretation alongside the Pesher's makes visible the range of live options in 1st-century Jewish interpretation of this single text.

---

## Why This Text Isn't in Your Bible

Pesher Habakkuk is not a biblical book — it is a commentary on a biblical book, written by and for a specific sectarian community. No ancient community considered it scriptural. It was not cited, transmitted, or known outside the Qumran library.

Canon formation in Judaism after 70 CE worked through rabbinic consensus around texts with demonstrated liturgical and instructional use in the broader Jewish community. The Qumran community was gone; its library was buried; its distinctive interpretive tradition did not survive into the mainstream. Even if the Pesher had been known, its content — with its specific claims about the Teacher of Righteousness as the divinely authorized interpreter of prophecy — would have made it a sectarian curiosity rather than a universally authoritative text.

For early Christianity, the situation is different but reaches the same conclusion. Christians were deeply interested in Habakkuk 2:4 — Paul quotes it twice. But they developed their own interpretation (faith in Christ) and had no access to the Pesher, which was buried. When the Pesher was rediscovered in 1947, it arrived as a historical artifact, not a candidate for inclusion in any canon.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 600 BCE | Habakkuk writes, responding to the rise of Babylon |
| c. 400–200 BCE | Habakkuk 1–2 circulates; the verse "the righteous shall live by faith" becomes significant in Jewish reflection |
| c. 168 BCE | The Kittim (Romans) arrive in Egypt by ship to block Antiochus IV — Dan 11:30 identifies Kittim = Rome |
| c. 175–150 BCE | The Hasmonean crisis; the Teacher of Righteousness and the Wicked Priest active (scholarly consensus) |
| c. 150–130 BCE | Qumran community established; the pesher method develops |
| c. 100–50 BCE | Pesher Habakkuk composed; manuscript written |
| c. 50 BCE | The Kittim identified as Romans specifically — Pompey's conquest of Jerusalem (63 BCE) is likely the formative event |
| c. 48–45 BCE | Most probable period for the Pesher's composition based on linguistic and historical analysis |
| c. 68 CE | Qumran community ends; scrolls hidden in caves |
| 1947 CE | Cave 1 discovered; 1QpHab among the original seven scrolls |
| 1950–1951 CE | 1QpHab published by Millar Burrows in Dead Sea Scrolls of St. Mark's Monastery |
| 1950s–present | Scholarly debate over identities of the Teacher, Wicked Priest, and Liar; the text becomes central to understanding the DSS community |

---

*HESED notes: Pesher Habakkuk is the interpretive key to the entire Qumran library. It shows how the community read Scripture — not as a text about the past, but as a coded message whose true referents had always been them, now, the last days. This is a hermeneutic of total confidence: every word the prophet wrote was ultimately about this community's crisis, this high priest's corruption, this teacher's persecution, this empire's advance. It is also a hermeneutic of total risk: when the community ended and the Teacher was gone and the Romans were still there, the interpretation collapsed with the community. What survived is the verse: "the righteous shall live by his faithfulness." Paul took it in a different direction. Hebrews took it in another. The Pesher took it in theirs. Habakkuk wrote it without knowing where it would go. All of which is exactly what column 7 says the prophets do.*
